title: Your out-of-sample data is spent once
summary: The untouched window that tells you whether a strategy works is destroyed the moment you use it to choose between strategies.
takeaways: A held-back test window gives an honest answer the first time you look at it, and a progressively more flattering one every time after.
Picking the best of several candidates on the same test window selects the luckiest candidate, not the best one.
Luck does not persist, so the candidate chosen that way is the one most likely to deteriorate when you fund it.
Do every test that does not need the held-back window first: parameter sensitivity, logic review, branch isolation.
The trades in a test window are not a forecast of future trades. Extremes get worse in both directions.

related_tools.label: Overfit Check
related_tools.note: Splits a real symphony into the era its author could tune against and the era nobody could.

sections.title: The one-shot problem
paragraphs: The standard advice for testing a strategy is to hold back a slice of history, build against everything before it, and then check the result against the slice you withheld. The logic is sound. Data your strategy has never seen cannot have been fitted to, so performance on it is an honest estimate.
It is honest exactly once.

The moment you look at the held-back window, decide you are not happy, go back and change something, and look again, that window has entered your development process. It is no longer data the strategy has never seen. It is data the strategy has been adjusted against, one decision at a time, and the adjustment happened inside your head rather than in a parameter, which is precisely what makes it invisible.

sections.title: Choosing the best candidate means choosing the luckiest
paragraphs: This is the part that surprises people, because it breaks a comparison that feels obviously fair.

Suppose you have two strategies and one untouched window. You test both and pick the one that did better. That seems like the correct use of a clean test. It is not, and the reason is worth following carefully.

Performance on any window is the sum of two things: how much real, repeatable structure the strategy captures, and how kindly that particular stretch of history happened to treat it. Call the second part luck. It is not a small term. Market data is mostly noise.

Now take the extreme case where both strategies are equally good. The difference between their results is then entirely luck. By picking the higher number, you have picked the luckier one, with certainty. And luck, by definition, does not repeat. So the strategy you selected is the one whose future performance will fall furthest from what you measured.

The same thing happens when you test one strategy repeatedly. Ten rounds of tweak-and-recheck against the same window is a competition between ten candidates, judged on a mixture of skill and luck. The winner is disproportionately lucky, and the number you wrote down is disproportionately optimistic.

sections.title: Why this gets blamed on the market
paragraphs: A strategy selected this way goes live and decays. The usual explanation is that the market changed, and the timing does look suspicious: it worked for years in testing and stopped working the week real money arrived.

Markets do change. But they change slowly, and they rarely change in the exact week you funded an account. The more ordinary explanation is that nothing changed at all. The backtest number was inflated by a selection process, the live result is what the strategy was always going to do, and the gap between them was manufactured during development rather than by the market afterwards.

sections.title: What to do before you spend the window
paragraphs: The practical conclusion is not that out-of-sample testing is useless. It is that the test is expensive and should be the last thing you do, not the first.

Everything that can be checked without it, check first. Does the logic have a reason to work that you can say out loud? Do the parameters survive being nudged? Does each branch earn its place when isolated? Does the strategy depend on an execution detail the platform cannot actually deliver? All of that can be examined on the data you built with, and all of it kills more strategies than the final test does.
By the time you look at the untouched window, you want to be as close to certain as you can get. You get one clean read.

sections.title: The flat top
paragraphs: One test deserves singling out because it is cheap, it does not consume the held-back window, and it catches a great deal.

Whenever a strategy has a tunable number, look at how performance behaves in the neighbourhood of the value you chose, not just at the value itself. Plot it if you can, or simply check the two values either side.

What you want is a flat top. Performance should be high at your value and still high just beside it, falling away gently as you move further. That shape says the strategy is responding to something real and broad.

What you do not want is a spike. If performance is excellent at 80 and mediocre at 79 and 81, nothing about the number 80 is meaningful. You have found a coincidence in this particular history, and the correct response is not to keep 80 but to distrust the whole branch.

sections.title: Test-window trades are not a forecast
paragraphs: One more trap, and it catches careful people because it follows from a true statement.

If a test window is genuinely untouched, the results on it are unbiased, meaning nothing is systematically pushing them up or down. People then reason that the trades in that window are a fair sample of trades to come, and start computing things from them: if the worst drawdown here was 25 percent, then 25 percent is roughly the worst to expect.

That does not follow. Unbiased means the centre is honest. It says nothing about the edges. The trades in any one window are themselves a random draw, and real experience spreads wider than a single draw suggests, in both directions. The good outcomes you have not seen yet are better than the best in your sample, and the bad ones are worse than the worst.

This matters most for the number people care about most. Drawdown probabilities estimated by resampling a single test window can understate the true chance of an extreme loss by a large multiple. Treat the worst drawdown in any backtest as a thing that happened, not as a floor under what can happen.

title: If you cannot explain why it works, it probably does not
summary: A strategy with great numbers and no explanation is usually a coincidence that has not been counted properly.
takeaways: Every strategy should come with a sentence saying why the edge exists. If you cannot write it, you have found a pattern rather than a reason.
The number that governs how much to trust a result is how many variations you tried, including the small ones you did not write down.
Nudging a lookback from 10 to 9 or 11 should barely move the result. If it moves a lot, the number was fitted to this history.
A strategy that depends on trading at an exact minute is not implementable on Composer, whatever the backtest says.
Testing and tweaking against the same history is itself the mechanism that produces overfitting.

related_tools.label: Overfit Check
related_tools.note: Measures whether a symphony's results survive outside the window its author could tune against.

sections.title: The question that deflates most strategies
paragraphs: There is a question that experienced traders ask about any new result, and it is not about the Sharpe ratio. It is: why do you think this makes money?

Not what the rules are. Why the edge should exist at all. Who is on the other side of the trade, and what are they doing that leaves something on the table for you? Is it a structural effect, like the daily rebalancing that erodes leveraged funds in choppy markets? A behavioural one, like the tendency to sell too hard into a panic? A risk you are being paid to carry, which will occasionally cost you?
If you can answer, you have a strategy with a thesis, and a thesis is something you can monitor. You will know what would have to stop being true for the strategy to stop working.
If you cannot answer, you have a pattern. Patterns are abundant in financial data and most of them mean nothing.

sections.title: Count the attempts, including the ones you forgot
paragraphs: The single most useful number for judging a backtest is one that almost nobody records: how many variations were tried before this one was kept.

People consistently underestimate it. A builder asked how many ideas they tested will say half a dozen, and mean six distinct concepts. But the honest count includes every lookback window swapped, every threshold moved, every ticker substituted, every date range adjusted, every branch added and removed. Counted properly, half a dozen is routinely hundreds.

This matters because the chance of finding something that looks good purely by accident rises with the number of attempts. Search hard enough through noise and you will always find a pattern worth keeping. It has no more edge than a lottery ticket that happened to win, and it will behave accordingly when funded.

This is the uncomfortable corollary: the effort you put into improving a strategy against its backtest is the same effort that overfits it. Diligence does not protect you here, because diligence is the mechanism.

sections.title: Nudge every number
paragraphs: The cheapest test available, and the one that eliminates the most bad logic, is to move each parameter slightly and see what happens.

Take a lookback window of 10 days and try 9 and 11. Take a threshold of 80 and try 79 and 81. A strategy responding to something real should barely notice. The market does not know which number you picked, and a genuine effect does not switch off between 79 and 80.

If a one-point change takes a meaningful bite out of the annualised return, that parameter was fitted to this specific history. The correct response is not to search for a sturdier number nearby. It is to treat the branch as unproven, because what the test revealed is that the result was never about the logic.
Where logic does survive the nudge, there is a second benefit: you now know a range rather than a point, and you can pick from the middle of it instead of the peak.

sections.title: Overfit to a system that does not exist
paragraphs: There is a second kind of overfitting that is easy to miss, because the strategy is not fitted to the data. It is fitted to an execution model the platform does not offer.

A backtest evaluates at a defined moment. Live trading happens in a window, and the exact moment within it is not yours to choose. So if a strategy's results depend on acting at one specific minute, and fall apart when that minute moves, the backtest is describing a strategy you cannot run. The logic might even be sound. It is simply not implementable here.
This is worth checking deliberately whenever a result looks unusually clean, because the symptom reads as success rather than failure.

title: Test one branch at a time
summary: A method for finding out what a single condition inside a symphony actually contributes, by replacing everything else with cash.
takeaways: Build a probe symphony containing only the branch you want to judge, with cash as the fallback. Everything it does is attributable.
Cash as the else-leg turns the backtest into a record of when the signal fired and what happened when it did.
Check whether the branch's contribution comes from many firings or from one lucky event.
Never judge a change on the full backtest alone. Use the date range to look at six to twelve month windows.
Keep an unmodified copy and plot it against the draft, so you are comparing two curves rather than remembering a number.

related_tools.label: Nodes
related_tools.note: Counts the branches in a symphony, which is a reasonable proxy for how much there is to isolate.

sections.title: Why a whole symphony cannot be judged at once
paragraphs: A large symphony is a stack of conditions, and its backtest is a single curve. That curve is the sum of every branch, which means a branch that actively loses money can be invisible as long as the others carry it.
You cannot fix what you cannot see, and you certainly cannot tune it. So before changing anything inside a large strategy, it is worth extracting the piece you care about and looking at it alone.

sections.title: The probe
paragraphs: Build a small separate symphony that contains only the path you want to examine, with its surrounding conditions intact, and put cash in every other position.

Suppose a strategy holds a volatility hedge when SPY is above its 200 day moving average and SPY's 60 day RSI is above 60. The probe keeps exactly those two conditions and the position they lead to, and routes everything else to a short-term treasury fund standing in for cash.

The result is a backtest in which every move is attributable. The strategy is flat except when this branch is active, so the equity curve is a direct record of when the signal fired and what happened next.

sections.title: What to read off it
paragraphs: How often does it fire? A condition that triggers four times in a decade is not a feature of the strategy, it is a bet on four specific events. That may be fine, but you should know you are making it.
What does it cost when it is wrong? The drawdown of the probe is the drawdown this branch contributes, with nothing else to disguise it.

Where do the gains come from? This is the question that matters most. If the branch's entire contribution arrives in one window, it is not a strategy component, it is a memory of that window. A hedge that pays for itself only in a single crash will not pay for itself in the next one unless the next one rhymes.
Then nudge the parameters. Try 59 and 61 day lookbacks against 60. Try 14 and 16 against 15. A branch worth keeping does not care very much.

sections.title: The slider is not optional
paragraphs: This is the discipline most often skipped, and the one that causes the most quiet damage.
Do not judge a change on the full backtest. Narrow the date range and step through history in six to twelve month windows.

Here is why. Suppose a signal fires twenty times over a decade, and you make a change that improves one of those firings dramatically. On the full curve, that single improvement can outweigh small degradations across the other nineteen, and the summary statistics will approve. You have made the strategy better at one thing that already happened and worse at the thing it does repeatedly.
Stepping through windows makes that visible immediately, because you see the change fail nineteen times instead of seeing one number improve.

sections.title: Always compare against a baseline copy
paragraphs: Before changing anything, duplicate the symphony. Edit the copy and leave the original untouched, then plot both on the same chart.

This sounds like bookkeeping and it is, but it replaces memory with evidence. Remembering that the annualised return used to be about 31 percent is not the same as seeing the two curves diverge in March of a particular year, which tells you where the change took effect and whether the effect was the one you intended.
The same applies to the probes. Keep the unmodified probe beside the modified one.

title: Your live trades will not match the backtest
summary: Some divergence between live trading and the backtest is unavoidable. How much of it you get is a design decision you make while building.
takeaways: A condition evaluated near its threshold can resolve differently live than in the backtest. This is normal and cannot be fully removed.
Selecting one ticker from a sort means any mismatch is a total mismatch. Selecting two or three turns the same event into a partial one.
Short lookback windows are twitchy. Ten days or more is a reasonable floor, five an absolute minimum.
When a range of values all backtest about equally well, take the middle, not the best.
Several baskets at staggered window lengths convert a single all-or-nothing decision into a vote.

sections.title: Where the gap comes from
paragraphs: A backtest evaluates conditions against settled historical data at a consistent moment. Live trading evaluates them against the market as it stands when the order window opens, which is not the same moment and not the same data.

Most of the time this makes no difference. The gap appears when a condition is close to its threshold. If a strategy acts on a 60 day RSI above 60, and the real value at decision time is hovering at 60.02, then a small move in the minutes around execution decides which branch runs. The backtest records one answer with hindsight. Live trading got the other.

This is not a bug, and no amount of care removes it entirely. Even a slow condition like a 200 day moving average will occasionally land on the line. What you control is how often you sit on a line, and how much rides on it when you do.

sections.title: The arithmetic of picking one versus picking three
paragraphs: The most effective single change is also the least obvious, and it is worth stating as arithmetic.

If a sort selects the top 1 asset from a list and that selection differs from the backtest, then 100 percent of the position is wrong relative to the simulation. There is nothing else in the allocation to be right.

If the same sort selects the top 3 and one of them differs, then roughly a third of the position is wrong and two thirds match. The same underlying event, the same near-tie between two assets, produces a fraction of the deviation.

Selecting one asset maximises the backtest, because with hindsight the single best performer beats a basket containing it. That is exactly why it is fragile. You are concentrating everything on the one decision most likely to resolve differently in practice.

sections.title: Slow the conditions down
paragraphs: Short lookback windows move fast, and something that moves fast crosses thresholds often. A 3 day RSI can swing far enough between the backtest's evaluation and your actual fill to change the branch.

Ten days or more is a sensible floor for most conditions, and five is the point below which you should expect frequent disagreement. This is not a claim that short windows carry no information. It is that the information has to survive contact with execution, and below a certain speed much of it does not.

sections.title: Take the middle of the range, not the peak
paragraphs: This connects directly to parameter sensitivity, and it is the practical reason to care about it.
Suppose thresholds of 79, 80 and 81 all backtest about equally well. The instinct is to keep whichever is marginally best. The better choice is the middle, because the middle has room on both sides.

A threshold at the edge of a range that works has nowhere to drift. A threshold in the centre can be missed slightly in either direction and still land somewhere the logic holds. You are buying tolerance with a small amount of backtested return, and tolerance is what live trading spends.

The corollary is that logic which falls apart when a window moves by one or two points should not be deployed at all. If the difference between 9 and 10 days is large, live trading will find that cliff on your behalf.

sections.title: Spread the decision across several baskets
paragraphs: The strongest structural defence is to stop making one decision.

Rather than a single basket selecting assets on a 10 day moving average, build three or four baskets over the same assets, using staggered windows: 5, 10, 15 and 20 days, perhaps with different indicators. Allocate across them.

No single threshold now controls the portfolio. When one basket resolves differently from its simulated version, it moves a quarter of the allocation rather than all of it, and the others are unlikely to be sitting on their own thresholds at the same moment. One mismatch in five positions is a 20 percent deviation, where the same event in a single basket design is a 100 percent deviation.
This costs backtested performance. It is insurance, and insurance has a premium.

sections.title: Then accept the rest
paragraphs: After all of this, your trades will still sometimes differ from the simulation, and chasing the last of that gap is not a good use of attention.

What matters is that the deviations are small and unbiased. If your thresholds sit in the middle of ranges that work, a mismatch is roughly as likely to help as to hurt, and over enough decisions the two sides should broadly cancel. If your thresholds sit on cliff edges, mismatches do not cancel, because one side of the cliff is much worse than the other.
The goal is not a strategy that tracks its backtest perfectly. It is a strategy that does not care very much when it fails to.

title: How much to invest in a symphony
summary: Strategies holding assets that cannot be bought in fractions will leave part of your money in cash. Here is how to find the amount that stops that mattering.
takeaways: If a symphony holds non-fractionable assets, a small account cannot fill the target allocation and the remainder sits in cash.
Idle cash does not just reduce returns, it breaks the comparison between your live results and the backtest.
Find the threshold with a short backtest at a deliberately small investment amount, then raise the amount until the cash drag is small.
Use a short date range. Over a long backtest the balance grows and you stop measuring the amount you actually started with.
Turn off subscription fees for this test. They belong to your account, not to the strategy, and they distort small-balance runs.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: Many assets used in Composer symphonies cannot be purchased in fractional amounts. When a strategy wants 20 percent of the portfolio in such an asset and 20 percent is not a whole number of shares, it buys what it can. The difference stays in cash.

On a large account this rounding is negligible. On a small one it is not. A symphony meant to hold four positions might hold two and a meaningful cash balance, which is a different strategy from the one you chose.

The second effect is the one that causes confusion later. If you are sitting in cash on many days, your live results will not track the backtest, and you will spend time looking for a fault in the strategy when the explanation is that you funded it below the amount it needs.

sections.title: Finding the number
paragraphs: The method is to run a deliberately unrealistic backtest and read the allocation table.

Run a short backtest, three months or so, in a mode that shows you the table of trades beneath the chart. Set the simulated investment to something small, a hundred dollars rather than the default. Disable subscription or platform fees for the run. Then look at how much of the balance is sitting in cash on each day.
Raise the investment amount and repeat until the cash left over on any given day is down to a couple of percent. That figure is roughly the minimum the strategy needs in order to behave like itself.
For symphonies holding several non-fractionable assets, the answer is frequently in the low thousands rather than the low hundreds.

sections.title: Why each step matters
paragraphs: Keep the date range short. This is the step people skip, and skipping it quietly invalidates the test. Over a multi-year backtest the balance compounds, so by the end you are no longer measuring the amount you started with. A hundred dollars that grew to four hundred will round into positions comfortably, and the test will tell you that a hundred dollars is enough when it is not.
Use a small starting amount. The whole point is to find where rounding starts to bite, and a large simulated balance hides it.

Disable the fees. Platform subscription costs attach to your account rather than to one strategy, and on a hundred dollar simulated balance they are large enough to dominate everything else you are trying to see.

sections.title: A caution on the details
paragraphs: The principle here is durable: rounding into whole shares sets a floor on what a strategy needs, and below that floor your results will not resemble the simulation.

The specific steps describe a platform that keeps changing. Which assets are fractionable, whether your particular account type supports fractional trading at all, and where the relevant columns appear in the interface have all moved before and will move again. Treat the procedure as the shape of the test rather than as a sequence of clicks, and check the current behaviour of your own account before concluding anything.

title: When a leveraged product disappears
summary: Leveraged and inverse funds can be closed by their issuers, and exchange traded notes can fail in ways a fund cannot. Both are design constraints, not trivia.
takeaways: Leveraged and inverse products are closed by issuers regularly, usually after the volatility that made them interesting.
An ETF closure gives you some weeks of notice, and you may not receive it if you bought the position recently.
An exchange traded note is unsecured debt of its issuer, which adds failure modes a fund does not have.
A halt on new note issuance can break the link to the underlying index, and the note can trade at a large premium while it is broken.
Low volume is itself a risk, because symphonies rebalance at market and thin books widen the spread you pay.

related_tools.label: K1 Lookup
related_tools.note: Fund structure and tax treatment for the tickers that appear in symphonies.

sections.title: These products are not permanent
paragraphs: A backtest implicitly assumes the assets in a strategy will keep existing. For broad index funds this is a safe assumption. For leveraged and inverse products it is not.

Issuers close these funds, and they do it in batches. The period following the 2020 market dislocation saw a wave of leveraged and inverse product closures, which is the pattern worth internalising: they tend to be shut down after the volatility that made them attractive, not before it.

Note also that an issuer deciding to exit a position may close both halves of a pair. If there is a problem with one side of a 3x and -3x pairing, the other can go with it, which matters if your strategy rotates between them.

sections.title: What a closure actually looks like
paragraphs: A fund closure is not instant. The issuer files with the regulator, notifies shareholders, and the fund is delisted some weeks later, typically on the order of a month or two.

That is enough warning to act, with one catch that affects automated strategies specifically. The set of shareholders to notify is determined at a point in time. If a symphony rotates into the position after that point, you may hold a fund that is being wound down without having received the notice, and a strategy that only occasionally touches an asset is exactly the case where this happens.
The practical defence is unglamorous: know which products your symphonies can rotate into, and check on the unusual ones periodically. The list is normally short.

sections.title: Notes are a different instrument
paragraphs: Exchange traded funds and exchange traded notes are used interchangeably in most strategy discussions, and for tracking purposes they often behave similarly. Structurally they are not the same thing at all, and the differences only show up under stress.
A fund holds assets. A note is an unsecured debt obligation of the issuing bank, promising to pay the return of an index. It holds nothing on your behalf. Four consequences follow.
Credit risk. If the issuer fails, you are a creditor, and the index being up is not relevant to what you recover.

Issuance risk. Issuers create new notes to meet demand. If an issuer suspends creation, usually for its own regulatory or capital reasons, the supply of notes is capped while demand is not, and the price can detach upward from the index it is supposed to track. This is not hypothetical: a widely used volatility note traded at a very large premium to its indicative value during a 2022 issuance halt, meaning buyers were paying far above what the product was worth.
Call risk. Many notes can be redeemed early at the issuer's discretion. The position can be closed for you at a time you did not choose.
Governance. A fund has a board with duties to shareholders. A note does not.

None of this makes notes unusable. It does mean that where a fund and a note track the same exposure, the fund is usually the better default, and that a strategy relying on a note should be one you are willing to monitor.

sections.title: Volume is a risk setting
paragraphs: Thin products deserve more suspicion than they usually get, for a reason specific to automated strategies.

Symphonies rebalance on a schedule and take the price available when they do. In a thinly traded product the gap between bid and ask is wide, and that gap is a cost you pay on entry and again on exit, every single rebalance. A strategy that trades frequently can hand over a meaningful fraction of its edge this way without any of it appearing in a backtest, which fills at historical closing prices and knows nothing about the book.

Low volume also predicts closure, since a fund that cannot gather assets is the one an issuer shuts. Where two products offer near-identical exposure, the more heavily traded one is usually the better choice twice over.

title: Why the bond leg failed in 2022
summary: Treasuries are the default hedge in a great many symphonies, and in 2022 they fell alongside equities. The reason is structural and worth understanding before you rely on one.
takeaways: Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions, because an older bond must be discounted to compete with newly issued ones.
The longer a bond's remaining life, the more its price moves for a given change in rates. This is duration.
Long-dated treasury funds are a bet on rates, not a general safety asset, and leveraged versions of them are that bet multiplied.
In 2022 rates rose quickly, so the usual hedge fell at the same time as equities. The hedge did not fail, it did what it always does.
Ultra-short treasury funds and long-dated treasury funds are both called bonds and behave almost nothing alike.

sections.title: Why a bond falls when rates rise
paragraphs: A bond is a promise to pay fixed amounts on a schedule. Suppose you hold one that pays 7 percent a year on a face value of a thousand dollars, with five years left to run.

Now suppose newly issued bonds of similar quality pay 8.5 percent. Nobody will buy your 7 percent bond for a thousand dollars, because the same money buys a better income stream elsewhere. Your bond still pays exactly what it promised. What has changed is the competition, and the only way to make it competitive is to lower its price.

That is the whole mechanism. The price falls until the return a new buyer earns, counting both the coupons and the gap between the discounted price and the face value repaid at maturity, matches what they could get elsewhere. Rates up, existing prices down, with no change in the bond's own terms and no default involved.

sections.title: Duration, and why it decides everything
paragraphs: The size of that price move depends on how long the bond has left to run.

A bond maturing in six months is barely affected, because the mispriced income stream only lasts six months and then you get your money back at face value. A bond maturing in twenty years is affected enormously, because the discount has to compensate for twenty years of paying below the going rate.

This sensitivity is called duration, and it is the single most useful property of a bond holding. It explains why two funds that both hold nothing but United States treasuries, with no credit risk in either, can behave like completely different asset classes.

It also explains the leveraged case. A 3x long-dated treasury fund is a long-duration rate bet with the sensitivity tripled, plus the usual erosion that leveraged funds suffer in choppy conditions. It is one of the more volatile instruments commonly used in symphonies, and it is often placed in the slot labelled safe.

sections.title: What actually happened in 2022
paragraphs: Treasuries earned their reputation as a hedge in a particular kind of downturn. Growth stalls, the central bank cuts rates to stimulate, and falling rates push bond prices up at the same time as equities fall. The two legs offset, which is the behaviour the hedge is bought for.

In 2022 the sequence ran the other way. The problem was inflation rather than stalling growth, so the policy response was to raise rates quickly rather than cut them. Rising rates push bond prices down. Equities fell for the same reason, and so the hedge fell with the thing it was hedging.

It is worth being precise about the lesson. The bond leg did not malfunction. It did exactly what the mechanism above says it must do when rates rise. What failed was the assumption that treasuries hedge equities in general, when what they actually hedge is a specific scenario.

sections.title: Funds have no maturity date
paragraphs: There is a difference between holding a bond and holding a fund of bonds that matters during exactly these episodes.
An individual bond held to maturity returns its face value, whatever happened to its price along the way. The loss from rising rates is real while you hold it, but it has an end date.

A fund has no maturity. It holds a rolling portfolio, selling bonds as they age and buying new ones, so there is no point at which it is pulled back to par. A decline in rate-driven value is simply a decline.

Flows can make this worse. When prices fall, investors sell, and if the fund lacks cash to meet redemptions the manager must sell holdings to raise it, at depressed prices. The selling is forced by other people's exits rather than by any view on value, and it happens at the worst available moment.

sections.title: What this means when you build
paragraphs: Treat the word bond as uninformative. The relevant question about any fixed income leg is its duration, because that determines what it is actually betting on.

An ultra-short treasury fund is close to cash. It barely moves with rates and it is a reasonable stand-in for sitting out. A long-dated treasury fund is a directional position on interest rates that happens to have no credit risk. A leveraged long-dated fund is that position amplified. These are three different decisions, and they are routinely described with the same word.

If a symphony's defensive leg is long duration, then the strategy has an embedded view on rates whether or not its author intended one, and it will struggle in any period where rates rise alongside falling equities. That is not a reason to avoid it. It is a reason to know it is there, and to check whether the backtest covers a period when rates did anything other than fall.
